extracted.intended_audience: improvisers, acting students and teachers (theatre/improv classes)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance and exercises for using status (high/low) in improvisation to create truthful characters, comedy, and dramatic dynamics; includes exercises (status ladders, competitions), coaching methods, and body-language rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eliminate fillers and unnecessary gestures
rubrics_metrics.description: Without being told to—the improvisers eliminated “ers” and “ums,” made fewer unnecessary gestures, sustained long pauses and so on.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These behaviors often arise unconsciously in response to status work; reducing filler words and needless movement makes performances more truthful and status signals clearer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine individual strong and weak status triggers
rubrics_metrics.description: Determining what is a strong and a weak status trigger for an individual will help them become truthful at any point on the status spectrum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an improviser consciously alters only one aspect of their behavior, their body will unconsciously—and therefore truthfully—adjust to match. Trainers should help students identify personal triggers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize body over dialogue for status information
rubrics_metrics.description: We get more status information from the body, so if the status of the dialogue and the body are not congruent, the body will tend to win.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When teaching or performing, ensure body language matches intended status; playing text against body (incongruence) can be used deliberately for effect, but unchecked mismatch undermines truthfulness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Play lines against implied status to refresh familiar roles
rubrics_metrics.description: Playing a line or a scene against its implied status can suddenly give it a fresh new life, especially if it’s a role that is well known or associated with an iconic performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliberately contrast the implied status of text and the actor’s physicality/attitude to create interest; useful for reviving well-worn parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize status gaps widen in high-stakes contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: In high-stakes situations, gaps in status tend to be widened (examples: military saluting/attention, hospitals' chains of command, Gordon Ramsay’s kitchen).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use wider status differentials to convey urgency, clear hierarchy or pressure; when stakes are lower, status gaps should generally be narrower.

rubrics_metrics.name: Titles and manner of address convey status
rubrics_metrics.description: When society wants to bestow status on someone they often give them a title. The 'Very Right Reverend Spacklington-Smythe' is a higher status name than 'Bob' because it takes all day to say.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use names, titles and forms of address as quick status markers; characters may level status by offering informal forms ('Call me Bob').

rubrics_metrics.name: Status can be lost in presence of higher-status individuals
rubrics_metrics.description: Some people who are normally very high status can lose it suddenly in certain situations (example: Madonna losing status in presence of royalty).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be alert to contextual status shifts; even normally high-status characters can become low-status depending on relational cues and setting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical size and posture signal status (animals example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Size equals high status: the cat made herself as large as she could, looked the fox in the eye and stood still; the fox was intimidated and left.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use posture, size-making and direct gaze as practical status signals; even when physically smaller, an actor can create high-status presence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Still head as a powerful high-status move
rubrics_metrics.description: Keeping your head still while speaking is a tremendously powerful high status move—too powerful for most normal purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice with partners: maintain eye contact and a still head while saying threatening lines; have partners coach whether head moved; use sparingly because of its extreme effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Status Ladder exercise (ascending)
rubrics_metrics.description: Four people enter a scene one at a time and form a Status Ladder, with each person who comes in being higher status than those who preceded them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a bland scenario to let characters reveal themselves strongly; prompt with open-ended lines (e.g., 'I've got something to tell you all') to start interaction. Works well to sustain audience interest despite minimal plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reverse Status Ladder exercise (descending)
rubrics_metrics.description: Same exercise but each person who enters has to be lower status than those who went before; host can set the bar by starting high or low.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Starting low can create 'space' under the host and produce neurotic/comedic characters (apologizing, etiquette obsessing). Use to explore low-status behavior for comic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Random-order Status Ladder (relative status choices)
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct a status ladder in a random order; entrants must decide relative to others (higher, lower, middle) and interact with those on stage before entering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This tests improvisers' flexibility; at scene end, ask audience/actors to order them—collisions are common and instructive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Status is relative — avoid absolute status assignments
rubrics_metrics.description: Status describes how we interact with others. It is meaningless to talk about 'absolute' status (e.g., 6 out of 13). With only two people you only know one is higher or lower; positions (1–4) depend on subsequent entrants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Train improvisers to think relationally; the same character may be 1 in one moment and 3 in another depending on others. Use the concept of the 'Kinetic Dance' (sharing space) to teach dynamism.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to play a convincing number 2
rubrics_metrics.description: To be a number 2 you need a number 1 you can submit to and a number 3 you can dominate; show a different side of yourself to number 1 than to number 3.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rather than summon an ineffable sense, demonstrate contrasting behaviors toward higher and lower partners; this clarifies the middle-status role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unnecessary status collisions (blocking)
rubrics_metrics.description: A status collision on the number 1 spot (two players both trying to be 1) is a particularly pernicious form of blocking. Once trained improvisers may never show vulnerability on stage, blocking scenes that need it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach vulnerability and discourage gratuitous status battles unless the game calls for them. Note: some games (e.g., Fight For Your Number) depend on collisions—use intentionally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extremes of status tend to create comedy; small gaps tend to create drama
rubrics_metrics.description: Two things are worth noticing: extremes of status usually lead to comedy where small status gaps tend to lead to drama.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose status gaps according to desired tone: for laughs, widen gaps; for tension/drama, keep gaps subtle.

rubrics_metrics.name: High-status competition setup (who's higher?)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two students play a scene where each must try to be more high status than the other (e.g., potential tenant vs. flat-owner). It’s important that one person isn’t trying to sell the flat, because that evens the status out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame it as a competition judged by the audience; watch for quick drops in status (big laughs). Encourage exploration—results teach about status relationships even if not 'successful.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Use status drops/slapstick for comic effect
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Man slips on banana peel' is the archetypal joke — a quick drop in status. If a high-status figure falls (e.g., the pope), it's funnier because of their endowed status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comedians may raise status immediately before a fall to maximize comic potential. Beware: a sustained, large status drop across acts becomes tragedy rather than comedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Happy high status — combine confidence with likability
rubrics_metrics.description: Marry high status body language with smiling, charming behavior: compliment others, never defend yourself, raise the status of others while maintaining your own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Happy high-status people can be generous (the Queen example). Practice being high status while being likable; this subtlety is valuable in character work and corporate training.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coaching by giving 'thoughts' rather than instructions
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective coaching: tell the improviser what you are thinking (e.g., 'You’re not in a hurry. I’m sure they’ll wait...') rather than step-by-step directions; 'He wasn’t telling her what to do. He was telling her what he was thinking!'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When coaches voice real thoughts, improvisers automatically know what to say and behave more truthfully; this produces human, obvious, and often hilarious choices. Use side-coaching to transfer a performer's gestalt to another.

rubrics_metrics.name: Train performers to be 'someone else' so they need less direction
rubrics_metrics.description: Once people have been trained to be someone else (via coaching/thoughts), they only need direction when they meet novel situations; use hand signals or occasional side-coaching as needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This method preserves performers' spontaneity while providing safety nets; it allows performers to improvise without being fed lines and reduces stopping to ask for clarification.

rubrics_metrics.name: As a teacher: don't rush conclusions but have answers when needed
rubrics_metrics.description: As a teacher, it is advisable not to rush the students to your conclusions—although if you set a problem it is good to have an answer, or you may frustrate the students.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow exploration and discovery time; guide toward success but not too quickly, unless pressed for time, to avoid missing valuable learning moments.
